title: Now Entering: The Era Of Bleh | NOEMA
gist: Aaron Horwath argues that 'AI for everything' adoption, with every firm in an industry routing its thinking through the same small ecosystem of LLMs such as Claude and ChatGPT, produces 'Airbrain': a homogenization of knowledge-work output and strategy that erodes competitive differentiation and atrophies human skills. He predicts a zag back to paid human uniqueness and a barbell-shaped, bifurcated knowledge-work market (near-zero-cost AI output vs. premium verifiably-human craft, hollowed-out middle, offshored human-in-the-loop roles), followed by a failed executive experiment with fractional, gig-style knowledge work.

themes.theme: Airbrain: LLM-driven homogenization of knowledge work

insights.claim: When competing companies in the same industry all run their thinking, strategy and content through agents built on the same small ecosystem of LLMs, it is effectively as if they had all hired the same single employee, so competitive differentiation erodes and the value proposition of firms paid for solutions only they can provide collapses.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: For services, agencies and SaaS firms whose moat is 'unique expertise', indiscriminate AI adoption can commoditize the product; watch for margin compression and pricing pressure among heavy AI adopters in the same vertical.
insights.quote: Almost as if all these companies have simultaneously hired the same single employee: Mr. Claude (or one of his contemporaries).

insights.claim: Horwath coins 'Airbrain' as the knowledge-work analogue of Kyle Chayka's 'AirSpace': just as Instagram and Foursquare algorithms flattened coffee shops, bars and Airbnbs into one generic aesthetic, widespread AI adoption is converging newsletters, websites and ads across competitors on the same Claude-aesthetic, tone of voice and way of articulating ideas.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Brand distinctiveness in marketing and content is becoming scarcer; firms with an identifiable human voice may gain relative attention share as AI-generated content saturates channels.
insights.quote: Newsletters, websites and ads across competitors and industries are converging on the same Claude-aesthetic, the same tone of voice and the same way of articulating ideas.

insights.claim: The em dash, overused by LLMs, has become a marker of 'AI slop', and its sudden prominence across knowledge-work output is a visible symptom of intellectual homogenization inside organizations.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Stylistic AI tells are becoming legible to audiences, which lowers the perceived value of AI-generated communications and raises the payoff of detectably human writing.

insights.claim: A 2026 PNAS Nexus study by Emily Wenger (Duke) and Yoed Kenett (Technion) tested 22 commercial LLMs against more than 100 humans on creativity tasks: individual models sometimes beat individual people, but as a population the LLMs converged on strikingly similar answers while humans did not.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Benchmarks of single-model quality miss the population-level diversity loss; an industry where everyone uses LLMs gets less idea variance, which matters for innovation-driven sectors.
insights.quote: Overreliance on these tools,” Wenger concluded, “will smooth the world’s work toward the same underlying set of words or grammar, tending to make writing all look the same.

insights.claim: Homogenization is structurally inevitable because LLMs are prediction machines that take a statistical guess at the likeliest next token, which pushes output toward the generic and strips out the idiosyncratic markers of a human author.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Differentiation cannot be bought by switching to a better model alone; durable edge must come from proprietary inputs, process and human judgment layered on top.

insights.claim: The problem is not limited to AI-generated content ('Workslop'): employees increasingly delegate higher-level work such as business-problem solutions, sales coaching, campaign strategy and stakeholder management to AI, meaning the homogenization reaches the foundations of a company's vision, direction and market perception.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Strategic convergence among competitors is a less visible but larger risk than content sameness; expect crowded, similar strategies across AI-heavy peers.

insights.claim: The Army Corps of Engineers straightened and dredged 103 miles of the Kissimmee River in central Florida between 1962 and 1971 to stop flooding; the loss of bends destroyed nearly 35,000 acres of floodplain habitat and roughly 90% of wintering waterfowl, and restoring 44 miles of bends from 1999 to 2021 cost more than $1 billion.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: An analogy for the cost of over-optimizing processes: efficiency gains that remove hidden functions can require far larger remediation spending later.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

insights.claim: AI straightens the 'bends' of organizational work (idea, stakeholder feedback, refinement, approval), letting individuals vibe-code apps, build dashboards and run analyses in isolation in hours; this turns knowledge work into something like manufacturing with humans as foremen, but those slow, meandering collaborative steps were what refined ideas and made solutions unique to the organization.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Productivity metrics for AI rollouts may overstate value; the hidden cost is lost innovation, which shows up with a lag in product differentiation and pricing power.
insights.quote: But manufacturing is no place for innovation.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

insights.claim: An organization's unique selling points are the aggregate unique talents of the people it hires, so assembling the right combination of people is the ultimate moat, and routing all of their work through AI filters out the talent the company paid for and customers expect.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: In evaluating people-intensive businesses, how AI is deployed relative to core talent matters more than headline adoption rates.
insights.quote: Building an organization with the right combination of people is, and always has been, the ultimate moat.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

insights.claim: Jay Barney (University of Utah) and co-authors argue in MIT Sloan Management Review that AI can give at most a short-term competitive advantage, because the value it unlocks is unlocked for everyone, making AI a source of homogenization rather than differentiation.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of equity stories that frame generic AI adoption as a durable moat; AI-driven margin gains are likely to be competed away across the peer group.
insights.quote: Far from being a source of differentiation, artificial intelligence will be a source of homogenization.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

themes.theme: Skill atrophy as a hidden liability

insights.claim: A 2026 Nature report found that skills atrophy very quickly after AI is introduced, and in a 2026 survey of 2,500 employees 39% said their reliance on AI was actively making them less intelligent.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Workforce deskilling is an unbooked liability for AI-heavy firms; reversing course later will carry retraining time and cost.
insights.quote: A 2026 Nature report found it takes shockingly little time for skills to atrophy once AI has been introduced.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

insights.claim: Organizations that adopted AI fastest and without limits face a path-dependency risk: when they later want to return to human-generated differentiation, they may need time to rebuild the very cognitive skills that differentiated them, so they should move now to a targeted approach that in some places adds back friction.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Favor companies that deliberately preserve human capability in core differentiating functions over those maximizing AI substitution everywhere.
insights.locator: Make it More Efficient …Wait! Not Like That!

themes.theme: The zag back to human uniqueness

insights.claim: Coffee-shop homogenization has been measured: in a study asking people to identify a cafe's location from a photo, no participant placed all six correctly and only 6% could distinguish Chicago from San Francisco; yet the cafe industry then pivoted to differentiated experiences because sameness stopped paying.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Precedent that homogenization cycles self-correct: once a market becomes interchangeable, uniqueness becomes the premium and spending shifts toward differentiated offerings.
insights.quote: the novelty of a product is now just as important as the product itself.

insights.claim: Once every player in an industry uses AI, its competitive advantage is neutralized, so knowledge-work firms will return to uniqueness in content, strategy and solutions as the source of advantage, and will again seek and pay for human judgment, perspective and taste that LLMs cannot provide.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Expect a re-rating of demand for senior creative, strategic and taste-driven talent after the AI adoption wave, and a premium for firms that can prove human-originated work.

insights.claim: Big consultancies are already signaling the shift: Deloitte's 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report says competitive advantage is now driven less by technology and more by cultivating the 'human edge', and EY has committed $100 million to reward employees who show adaptability, innovation and judgment.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Large professional-services firms are putting money behind human differentiation, an early sign that AI-era talent spend is shifting toward judgment-heavy roles.
insights.quote: Technology — especially something as increasingly ubiquitous as AI — is replicable. People aren’t.

insights.claim: Erin McGurk and David Khachaturov (Cambridge, 2026) describe a barbell concentration of value in AI-saturated markets: AI-produced assets at near-zero marginal cost on one end, verifiably human-origin products sold at a premium on the other, and a hollowed-out middle, forcing most organizations to choose cheap high-volume AI production or low-volume high-value craft.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Mid-market, mid-priced knowledge-work providers are the most exposed; human-provenance verification and certification emerge as potential infrastructure plays.
insights.quote: Most importantly, the middle will hollow out.
insights.locator: Twin Peaks: A Bifurcation Of Knowledge Work

insights.claim: 'Human in the loop' oversight roles will mostly shift to lower-cost labor markets, because a worker with clear instructions and a Claude account can produce or evaluate the same homogenized output far more cheaply than a premium employee.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Supports demand for offshore BPO and AI-review labor platforms while pressuring wages for onshore mid-level knowledge workers.
insights.locator: Twin Peaks: A Bifurcation Of Knowledge Work

insights.claim: AI companies themselves hint at the future shape of work: Anthropic is hiring highly paid tastemakers and ChatGPT is hiring an Employer Brand Manager among other strategy-defining roles, while the industry trend of merging developer, designer and product manager into one 'builder' role collapses three jobs into one taste-defining role with AI filling technical gaps.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Role consolidation implies headcount reduction in tech product teams even as pay for the surviving taste-heavy roles rises.
insights.quote: If we start to see three roles combined into one, what happens to the other two?
insights.locator: Twin Peaks: A Bifurcation Of Knowledge Work

insights.claim: In a bifurcated knowledge-work market, a small group of tastemakers and visionaries will capture a growing share of the salary pie, similar to the widening wealth gap, and will be evaluated on quality and novelty rather than output volume.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Expect superstar-style pay dispersion inside white-collar professions; the social and political fallout from mid-tier white-collar displacement is worth watching.
insights.quote: The future of knowledge work, then, will be ruthlessly bifurcated.

themes.theme: Fractional workforce experiment and the doorman fallacy

insights.claim: As human work shrinks to lower-volume tastemaking and agent review, executives will be tempted by spreadsheets showing 70% salary reductions to try an Uber-like fractional model for knowledge work; Upwork's Future of Work Index 2026 reports skilled freelancing rose from 28% of skilled knowledge workers in 2025 to 38% in 2026, and Gartner predicts that by 2027 more than 30% of midsize enterprises will have at least one fractional executive on retainer.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Tailwind for freelance and fractional-talent marketplaces in the near term as companies pursue AI-plus-gig cost cutting.
insights.quote: skilled freelancing rose from 28% of skilled knowledge workers in 2025 to 38% in 2026.

insights.claim: Horwath argues the AI-plus-gig model will fail in the long run because of Rory Sutherland's 'doorman fallacy': defining a job by its notional task ignores context, relationships, institutional knowledge and trust, and an organization made mostly of fractional workers is not really an organization, though many executives will learn this only after businesses have been gutted.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Be wary of companies announcing aggressive AI-plus-fractional headcount cuts; the savings may reverse through lost institutional knowledge and customer value.
insights.quote: an organization composed of overwhelmingly fractional workers isn’t an organization at all

insights.claim: The next AI era requires replacing the blunt 'AI for Everything' strategy with deliberate choices: which roles and tasks are strictly human, how AI supports differentiating work, which areas are carved out as 'AI-Free', and which friction should be removed versus which friction makes the best work possible.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging management quality on AI: selective, differentiated deployment beats blanket mandates.
